To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Cα subunits of cAPK and Ca2+-calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) are expressed in E. Coli as active protein kinases that have kinetic parameters similar to their mammalian tissue counterparts.

prokaryotic production of the cAMP-dependent protein kinase catalytic subunit yields a protein with kinetic properties and phosphorylation characteristics identical to the native enzyme, and that the purified recombinantly produced enzyme has been used to solve the three-dimensional structure of the protein kinase.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structure-function relationships of the catalytic subunit (Cα) of cAMP-dependent protein kinase.
understanding the mechanism of action of the catalytic subunit (Cα) of the cyclic AMP-dependent protein kinase (cAPK).
the structure, function, and mechanism of protein kinase C (PKC) isoforms and their role in the regulation of cellular functions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the C subunit is a soluble protein in E. coli, and that it is a phosphoprotien.
prokaryotic systems have not been successful in the production of active, soluble protein kinases.
the expression of the C subunit is a viable system for the production and study of the cAPK enzyme.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the C subunit is an extremely difficult protein to express and purify, but that the methods presented in this chapter will allow the production of milligrams of active, soluble protein with a high degree of success.
we have successfully produced milligrams of active, purified, recombinant C subunit of the mammalian cAPK in E. coli and have used it for crystallization.

we have been successful in expressing a catalytic subunit in a heterologous system that is active in vitro and in vivo, and that the protein has been crystallized and the three-dimensional structure determined.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Cα subunits of PKA can be produced in large quantities in E. coli with little difficulty and that these proteins are fully functional.
the expression of protein kinase in bacteria is a viable approach to the production of large amounts of protein.
it should be possible to produce a functional, active, and soluble protein kinase in E. coli by following a few simple steps.
